title: IDRF: Inverse-Distilled Reward Fine-tuningof Masked Discrete Diffusion Models

paper.title: IDRF: Inverse-Distilled Reward Fine-tuning of Masked Discrete Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Masked discrete diffusion models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive generation, but iterative sampling can be costly, and intractable sequence likelihoods complicate reward fine-tuning. We introduce IDRF , a framework for reward fine-tuning of few-step masked discrete diffusion generators. Starting from a standard reverse-KL-regularized objective, IDRF replaces the intractable sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization. With an optimal auxiliary denoiser, we prove that the population inverse-distillation loss upper-bounds the sequence-level KL divergence to the reference distribution. IDRF optimizes a trajectory-based surrogate of this loss without reference-model rollouts, so the student keeps its own few-step sampler. We view few-step generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and optimize reward with a clipped policy-gradient objective over the student’s trajectories. Across DNA, image, and text generation, IDRF achieves high reward with up to 32 × 32\times fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate sequences by unmasking tokens in parallel, with applications to language, biological sequences, and discrete image representations ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . Reward fine-tuning adapts these models to task objectives, such as DNA activity, image attributes, or review sentiment. Optimizing reward alone, however, can destroy properties the reward does not measure (Figure 1 ). KL regularization toward a pretrained reference provides a standard safeguard ( Ziegler et al., 2019 ; Korbak et al., 2022 ) , but an MDM’s sequence likelihood marginalizes over all denoising trajectories and is intractable. Existing reward fine-tuning methods use likelihood surrogates and evidence bounds ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) , or penalize KL between reverse transitions ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . The latter requires reference evaluations along the rollout and ties the regularizer to its sampling path. We seek a tractable sequence-level KL regularizer that lets the student use its own sampler. We introduce Inverse-Distilled Reward Fine-tuning (IDRF) , which combines trajectory-based policy gradients with inverse distillation ( Li et al., 2026 ) . The regularizer compares the denoising losses of a frozen reference and a fitted auxiliary on student samples. It requires neither the reference’s likelihood nor its rollouts. Both the reward and the regularizer reuse the student’s own trajectories (Figure 2 ), so the regularizer shapes the student’s few-step sampler directly. Reward fine-tuning requires neither pretraining data nor reward gradients. Our contributions are as follows. 1. With an optimal auxiliary denoiser, we establish a sequence-level KL bound for the population inverse-distillation objective in masked diffusion, valid for any sequence length and any student sampler ( \wasyparagraph 3.1 ). 2. We regularize reward fine-tuning with a practical inverse-distillation objective on the student’s own trajectories, without reference rollouts. The resulting framework supports reward fine-tuning directly in the few-step regime ( \wasyparagraph 3.2 ). 3. Across DNA, images, and text, IDRF reaches high reward with up to 𝟑𝟐 × \boldsymbol{32\times} fewer denoising steps than the reference while preserving properties lost under reward-only fine-tuning ( \wasyparagraph 5 ).

sections.heading: 2 Background
sections.text: This section reviews the two ingredients of IDRF. \wasyparagraph 2.1 introduces masked diffusion and the NELBO used to pretrain the reference, and \wasyparagraph 2.2 describes inverse distillation, which IDRF turns into a regularizer for reward fine-tuning.

sections.heading: 2.2 Inverse Distillation
sections.text: IDLM uses inverse distillation to train a fast discrete generator from a pretrained denoiser ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Pretraining fits a denoiser to a given data distribution. Inverse distillation reverses this direction by fixing the reference denoiser f ref f_{\mathrm{ref}} and learning a student distribution p θ p_{\theta} on which its predictions remain optimal. In the ideal setting, a student matching p ∗ p^{*} would produce samples that the reference can denoise as well as any model fitted specifically to those samples. A low reference loss alone is not enough to ensure this match. For example, a student that repeats a single sequence may be easy to denoise despite covering very little of the data distribution. Inverse distillation accounts for how predictable the student’s samples are by comparing the reference with the best denoiser for those same samples. This gives the objective ℒ ID ​ ( θ ) = ℒ NELBO ​ ( f ref , p θ ) − min f ⁡ ℒ NELBO ​ ( f , p θ ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ID}}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NELBO}}(f_{\mathrm{ref}},p_{\theta})-\min_{f}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NELBO}}(f,p_{\theta}). (4) Minimizing this gap encourages the student to produce samples on which refitting the denoiser offers little improvement over the reference. This objective also has a distribution-matching guarantee. With a Bayes-optimal reference for p ∗ p^{*} and an exact inner minimum over a sufficiently expressive denoiser family, IDLM shows ( Li et al., 2026 , Theorem 3.1) ℒ ID ( θ ) ≥ D KL ( p θ ∥ p ∗ ) ≥ 0 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ID}}(\theta)\geq D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{\theta}\,\|\,p^{*}\right)\geq 0, (5) so a zero gap means that the student matches the data. IDLM proves this bound for a single token and for a joint reverse process over whole sequences, and leaves the sequence objective used in practice, a sum of per-token denoising losses, to future work ( Li et al., 2026 , App. D.2) . Proposition 1 proves the bound for its population loss and an arbitrary reference. In practice, a trainable auxiliary denoiser f ψ f_{\psi} approximates the inner minimum by learning to reconstruct masked student samples. Training alternates between fitting the auxiliary and updating the student to reduce the difference between reference and auxiliary losses. The reference remains fixed throughout. IDRF uses this denoising gap as the regularizer for reward fine-tuning.

sections.heading: Why the population loss.
sections.text: Proposition 1 holds for any sequence length and any student sampler (Appendix A ). Replacing the KL in Eq. ( 6 ) by the population loss therefore gives a lower bound on the KL-regularized objective and motivates the regularizer of IDRF.

The prediction x ~ \widetilde{x} serves as a soft target on the simplex ( Li et al., 2026 ) , so each cross-entropy in ℒ NELBO \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NELBO}} becomes − ∑ v ∈ 𝒱 x ~ ℓ ( v ) log f ℓ ( v ∣ z ) -\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\widetilde{x}^{\ell}(v)\log f^{\ell}(v\mid z) for f ∈ { f ref , f ψ } f\in\{f_{\mathrm{ref}},f_{\psi}\} and a fresh corruption z z whose visible tokens are drawn from x ~ \widetilde{x} . At revealed positions, x ~ \widetilde{x} is the one-hot copied token. Sampling j j along the trajectory regularizes the student on the states its sampler visits, using a single auxiliary across depths. In our ablations, on-policy states work best: forward-masking completed student samples lowers ATAC-Acc from 95.3 % 95.3\% to 52.5 % 52.5\% in DNA design (Appendix C.4 ). The regularizer costs one student evaluation plus one forward pass through each of the reference and auxiliary models. We use a semi-gradient update for the inverse-distillation term: rollout states and sampled corruption contexts are held fixed, and gradients flow only through the student’s soft target probabilities. sections.heading: Distillation of masked diffusion models.
sections.text: Several methods reduce the sampling steps of a pretrained masked diffusion model. SDTT distills multiple teacher steps into fewer student steps ( Deschenaux & Gulcehre, 2025 ) , and Duo adapts consistency distillation to uniform-state discrete diffusion ( Sahoo et al., 2025 ) . Distribution-matching methods instead train a few-step generator to match the teacher’s distribution, through an integral KL objective in DiDi-Instruct ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) or inverse distillation in IDLM ( Li et al., 2026 ) . These methods reproduce the teacher, whereas IDRF (ours) uses inverse distillation to stay close to it while optimizing a reward.

sections.heading: Reward fine-tuning of masked diffusion models.
sections.text: To handle intractable sequence likelihoods, d1 and wd1 use denoising likelihood approximations ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2026 ) , while SPG uses lower and upper evidence bounds ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . Beyond reward fine-tuning, TUBE provides a further upper bound on the evidence of masked diffusion models ( Ivanov et al., 2026 ) . Alternatively, AGRPO treats denoising as an MDP with tractable stepwise action probabilities ( Zhan, 2026 ) , and TraceRL updates policies along recorded inference trajectories ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . DMPO and Discrete Tilt Matching learn reward-tilted distributions ( Zhu et al., 2026c ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . DRAKES instead uses differentiable relaxations for biological sequence design when reward gradients are available ( Wang et al., 2025a ) .

sections.heading: Joint distillation and fine-tuning.
sections.text: In continuous diffusion, Diff-Instruct++ regularizes one-step reward optimization with an integral KL ( Luo, 2025 ) , DMDR combines distribution matching with reinforcement learning ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , and RTDMD uses reward-tilted distribution matching for few-step flow generators ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . For masked image diffusion, Soft-Di[M]O refines a one-step generator through soft embeddings. Its adversarial refinement uses real images, and its reward fine-tuning requires differentiable rewards ( Zhu et al., 2026b ) . IDRF (ours) uses inverse distillation as the regularizer of trajectory-based policy gradients, supports reward fine-tuning directly in the few-step regime, and requires neither pretraining data nor reward gradients.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate IDRF on regulatory-DNA design, CLIP-guided image generation, and sentiment steering of review text. Across these tasks, we study its ability to achieve high reward with few sampling steps and preserve sample quality through inverse-distillation regularization.

sections.heading: Accessible, high-activity sequences in eight steps.
sections.text: With eight steps, IDRF attains the top ATAC-Acc in Table 1 with ancestral decoding ( 95.3 % 95.3\% , on par with 94.8 % 94.8\% for SDPO), and its max-confidence variant reaches the second-highest activity ( 7.31 7.31 ). Every baseline samples in 128 128 steps, 16 × 16\times more than IDRF. The one method with higher activity, SEPO + GF ( 7.66 7.66 ), keeps only 47.4 % 47.4\% of its sequences accessible, and SDPO reaches activity 6.30 6.30 .

sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Limitations
sections.text: We introduced IDRF, a framework for reward fine-tuning of few-step masked discrete diffusion models using inverse-distillation regularization. Across DNA, image, and text generation, IDRF achieves high reward with fewer sampling steps while mitigating reward hacking. Future work includes scaling IDRF to larger models and extending it to additional domains.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: In practice, IDRF involves an adversarial min–max game between the student and the auxiliary denoiser. As in other adversarial training methods, this can introduce optimization instability and sensitivity to the balance between their updates. The auxiliary also adds training cost. Our practical surrogate admits a related KL guarantee for a mixture of one-step completion distributions, while controlling the final sampling distribution remains an open question.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: AI tools assisted with language editing, code implementation, computational checks, and mathematical analysis during preparation. The authors are responsible for the claims, results, and final manuscript.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work develops a method for reward fine-tuning of masked diffusion models and involves no human subjects. All experiments use public datasets and pretrained models: the enhancer activity data of Gosai et al. (2024) , the ImageNet-trained MaskGIT ( Chang et al., 2022 ) , and the Amazon Reviews 2023 corpus ( Hou et al., 2026 ) . We do not redistribute review text. The DNA sequences are scored only by predictive models and were not synthesized or tested experimentally. Reward fine-tuning is dual-use. In particular, steering text toward a target sentiment could be misused to produce deceptive reviews at scale, and our sentiment experiment serves only as a benchmark for reward hacking.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: Reference is the pretrained model without fine-tuning. Classifier guidance (CG, Nisonoff et al., 2025 ) and two sequential Monte Carlo methods ( Wu et al., 2023a ) steer it at inference, SMC with the pretrained model as proposal and the twisted diffusion sampler (TDS) with CG as proposal. Classifier-free guidance (CFG, Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) samples a separately trained reward-conditioned model with guidance, as in DRAKES. D 2 -DPO ( Borso et al., 2025 ) and VRPO ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) adapt offline preference optimization to discrete diffusion. DRAKES ( Wang et al., 2025a ) backpropagates the reward through the generated trajectory with Gumbel-softmax relaxations. diffu-GRPO ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) and SEPO ( Zekri & Boullé, 2025 ) are policy gradient methods, with SEPO + GF denoting its gradient flow (GF) variant. DDPP-IS ( Rector-Brooks et al., 2025 ) matches the reward-tilted posterior with importance sampling, and SDPO ( Han et al., 2026 ) decomposes trajectory alignment into stepwise objectives.

sections.heading: Data and SFT.
sections.text: We use the Amazon Fashion split of the Amazon Reviews 2023 corpus ( Hou et al., 2026 ) . We remove duplicate reviews after trimming leading and trailing whitespace. Each training sequence contains a single review. We retain nonempty reviews with at most 126 126 GPT-2 tokens and reserve 1 % 1\% for validation using a deterministic hash-based split, without truncation or sentiment filtering. Each training sequence starts with bos , followed by the review text, and is padded with eos tokens to length 128 128 . All 127 127 non-BOS positions are noised and supervised. The reward is the log-probability of the one-star class under the frozen classifier https://huggingface.co/LiYuan/amazon-review-sentiment-analysis . Starting from the MDLM OpenWebText checkpoint ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) with the GPT-2 tokenizer, we run EOS-aware SFT for 50,000 50{,}000 steps at learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} and take the EMA weights. SFT uses Adam with global batch size 512 512 , 2,500 2{,}500 warmup steps, EMA decay 0.99 0.99 , and seed 42 42 . This single checkpoint initializes the frozen reference, the student and the auxiliary denoiser for every reward fine-tuning run reported in Table 3 .

sections.heading: Reward fine-tuning.
sections.text: Rollouts use ancestral sampling followed by a stochastic categorical terminal step, so K K reverse updates cost K + 1 K+1 denoiser evaluations. The score-function estimator of Eq. ( 20 ) is applied to the full trajectory without subsampling reverse steps. Each rollout batch receives a single on-policy update, so θ = θ old \theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}} and the clipping in Eq. ( 10 ) is inactive here. Groups contain 8 8 rollouts per device, for a global batch of 64 64 across 8 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Both models are trained with Adam at a learning rate of 10 − 6 10^{-6} with 100 100 warmup steps. The auxiliary is updated once per student update. Evaluation runs every 100 100 updates on 1,000 1{,}000 fresh samples, and weights are checkpointed every 500 500 updates. The reward and GenPPL are read from the text up to the first EOS, while the RLOO and inverse-distillation losses are computed on the full length- 128 128 buffer, including the EOS tail. Every run starts from the same SFT checkpoint with training seed 0 0 , and IDRF uses λ ID = 0.01 \lambda_{\mathrm{ID}}=0.01 . IDRF16 is trained separately from IDRF32. All fine-tuned text models are evaluated after 10,000 10{,}000 updates.

The real-review rows score 1,000 1{,}000 held-out reviews that are disjoint from the GM reference. GenPPL is the exponential of the token-averaged GPT-2-large NLL across all reviews, using BOS as context and including one EOS per review. Norm. entropy is the Shannon entropy of the GPT-2 token frequencies within a sample divided by the log of its length, averaged over samples. BOS and EOS are excluded, and normalized entropy is set to zero for reviews containing fewer than two tokens. Repeated words account for a median of 66 % 66\% of word occurrences in RLOO reviews, 14 % 14\% in IDRF reviews, and 9 % 9\% in real one-star reviews. Word repetition is the fraction of word occurrences beyond their first occurrence, computed case-insensitively and summarized by the median across reviews.

sections.text: GM adapts the centered estimator of Hoogeboom et al. (2026, Eq. 14) to variable-length text. For a candidate set and a reference set of 1,000 1{,}000 reviews each, we compute the mean gradient of GPT-2-large’s token NLL on two disjoint subsets of 50 50 reviews each from each set and take the inner product of the two candidate-minus-reference differences. The reported value averages 10 10 such estimates, with one standard error across them. Each review contributes its mean token NLL, conditioned on BOS and including one EOS. Gradients are computed in float32 and inner products in float64. The estimator is unbiased for the squared distance between mean gradients, so two samples of the same distribution score zero in expectation. Table 10 uses two references from the held-out validation split. One holds 1,000 1{,}000 of the 2,748 2{,}748 eligible real one-star reviews, and the other 1,000 1{,}000 of the 21,448 21{,}448 real reviews of every rating. Each reference is compared against a disjoint sample of the same distribution, and both real-versus-real estimates ( 0.03 0.03 and 0.06 0.06 ) are consistent with zero. Against both references, IDRF at 32 32 steps has a 2.4 2.4 – 2.7 × 2.7\times lower GM than reward-only fine-tuning. These results suggest that inverse-distillation regularization reduces distributional drift under reward fine-tuning.
